job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm in the second term of a master's in structural engineering at Aldmoor University. Mornings are lectures on bridge dynamics, afternoons are in the lab with my study group, and I cycle home to the flat I share with two other students. My bachelor's was civil engineering, and I did internships at a surveying firm and at the city council's roads office. I like drawing by hand first and checking the numbers twice, and what wears me out is group projects where somebody pastes in software output they don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd say fine, good, because hype fades and engineers will still be signing off drawings. I'd tell my friends that a bridge doesn't care what the press release says. Online I'd probably stay quiet, I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plans stay as they are. I finish the master's, I apply to the big structural firms in the city, and I get chartered the normal way with a mentor. My dad is a bus driver and my mum cleans offices, so the family backing I have is real money they saved for me, and I don't want to waste it on a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the course and apply to about fifteen firms in the spring, mostly ones I did placements with. I'd keep my notebook habit and my hand calculations. In the first year of work I'd join the engineers' union branch, because I want someone on my side when pay talks come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the ground stays solid, which I like. I do worry a bit that I'm too slow with new tools, but nobody is forcing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Is that a choice, or just not got round to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a choice, partly. I watched a classmate submit a beam design from a chatbot and it had the load going the wrong way, and he didn't see it. I'd rather be slow and know why my answer is right. If the firm demands it, I'll learn, but I won't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still keeps you up, even though AI barely matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Rents in the city are climbing, and my master's ends just as the council freezes graduate hiring every few years. My parents' savings cover me for now, but I don't want to lean on my mum and dad forever. So I'd say the money worry is the old one, not the AI one.

say: I'd say the hype will fade and **engineers** still sign off the drawings.
Online I'd stay quiet, and with friends I'd joke that a bridge ignores press releases.
think: My plans hold: finish the **master's**, apply to big structural firms, and get chartered with a mentor.
The only real worry is city **rents** and the council's stop-start graduate hiring.
do: Apply to about **fifteen firms** in the spring, mostly ones I already did placements with.
Join the engineers' **union branch** in my first year at work.
feel: **Calm**, with a small nag that I'm slow with new tools.
S0.quote: I'd rather be slow and know why my answer is right.
fieldNote: Her **calm** comes from a strong cushion and plenty of local jobs, not from any trust in technology.
Avoids **AI tools** by principle after seeing a classmate's flawed bridge design.
Ordinary **money worries** (rent, council hiring freezes) outweigh AI worries here.

steps.text: Finish the structural engineering master's at Aldmoor without changing course
Send applications to fifteen structural firms in the spring
Join the engineers' union branch after starting work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and that the people at the top are getting the gains. At work I'd say my firm needs a plan for the juniors, because the checking and drafting jobs that train us are exactly what gets automated. To friends I'd say we need rules, like a duty to keep apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: it hits me sooner than I admit. A lot of what a graduate does in year one is checking calculations and producing drawings, and that is the type of thinking work the card says software takes first. I could be one of a smaller intake, and I'd be at a firm that's hiring two juniors where it hired six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using one AI tool after all, a structural calculation checker the firm approves, so I'm not the slow one. I'd ask my master's tutor for a placement in a site office, where judgement matters more. And I'd go to my union's meeting about graduate intake targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed at myself for resisting. I'm not scared for my job today, but the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the person who avoided AI and then picks it up under pressure. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, I'd rather choose it than be pushed. But I'd pick one narrow tool and understand it fully, like I do with a design code. Being pushed hurts less if I start before the deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Idris, who did computing and wants to be a junior developer. His entire first job is what the card says gets taken. I'd also worry about the technicians at the firm who do drawing office work, because they're not on a graduate salary with a family cushion like me.

say: I'd say the **gains** go to the top, so firms need a plan to keep training juniors.
I'd tell friends we need **rules**, like a duty to keep taking on apprentices.
think: Year-one checking and drawing is exactly the **thinking work** that software takes first, so my intake could shrink.
I could join a firm that hires **two juniors** where it used to hire six.
do: Learn one **approved calculation checker** so I'm not the slow one.
Ask my tutor for a **site-office placement** where judgement matters more, and attend the union's intake meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** and annoyed at herself for resisting, but not scared for her own job today.
S1.quote: I'd pick one narrow tool and understand it fully, like I do with a design code. Being pushed hurts less if I start before the deadline.
fieldNote: Public line is about **fairness** and union rules; private line is about her own thin year-one intake.
First visible **crack** in her AI refusal: a narrow, understood tool is acceptable.
Worries about **technicians** and her friend Idris more than herself.

steps.text: Learn one approved structural calculation checker before graduating
Ask the tutor for a placement in a site office
Go to the union meeting about graduate intake targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that governments are asleep. I'd tell my union branch to demand a plan in writing, with wage support and a pause on firing juniors. And I'd say it publicly even though I'm usually quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree loses its edge before I've used it. If thinking work is done better and cheaper in 2028, a structural engineer's calculations are first in line, and I'd have just finished a master's with only the site judgement part left. I have money and no debt, but I have no idea what the job is by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop avoiding the tools and spend the whole summer learning them properly, plus finishing my chartership route early. I'd ask my parents to keep their savings untouched and I'd live cheaply in the flat. After 2028 I'd take any site role I could get, because hands-on work gets 3 more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like a train I can see and can't slow. I'm more scared than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long for a master's plus chartership. Would you change the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might leave after the first year and take a site job, which would upset my tutor. Being on a building site seems safer than a screen right now, and the card says robots for hands-on work are about 3 years behind. I don't want to quit, but I'd rather be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum and dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad I'm sorry that I may not be the engineer they pictured, and that I still have their money safe. My dad always said a skill is something nobody can repossess. I'd have to say I'm not sure that's true any more.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** and governments are asleep.
I'd push my union branch to demand a written plan, **wage support** and a pause on firing juniors.
think: My degree may lose its edge before I use it, since structural **calculations** go first.
I have savings and no debt, but no idea what the **job** is by 2028.
do: Spend the summer learning AI tools properly and finish the **chartership** route early.
Take a **site job** after my first master's year, since hands-on work gets about 3 extra years.
feel: **Anxious**, like watching a train she can't slow, and more scared than she'd say aloud.
S2.quote: My dad always said a skill is something nobody can repossess. I'd have to say I'm not sure that's true any more.
fieldNote: Strong **cushion** keeps her anxious rather than alarmed, but the lack of any plan frightens her.
Willing to **leave** the master's early for site work: a big shift for someone who prefers the familiar.
Quiet person becomes publicly **political** when pushed.

steps.text: Spend the summer learning AI tools properly
Take a site engineering job after the first master's year
Push the union branch for a written wage-support plan
Leave my parents' savings untouched and live cheaply in the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sort of time you can fight with. I'd say to friends that we should be building the rules now, not after the fact. And at the council I'd say graduate hiring should be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be fine until about 2031, then not sure. I'd be about 29, which is an awkward age to have to start again. But I'd have done a few years on real sites, and judgement is the last thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a site-based graduate job and get chartered by about 2029. I'd learn AI tools in my first year, the checker my firm approves. I'd also save most of my pay, since my parents did without for me and I want to repay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not panic, there's runway, but I can't stop thinking about 2031 and being 29.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd do now, compared with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I wouldn't quit the master's. I'd have time to finish properly and get a name in a firm. With 2 years I'd be rushing for the nearest safe thing, here I can choose the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save most of your pay. What would that money be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit on a small flat, honestly, and maybe a few months of cover in case my firm cuts my team. It's a cushion for me, so my parents never have to bail me out. I'd like to buy something real before it all gets weird.

say: I'd say five years is **time to fight** and the rules must be built now.
think: I'd be fine until about **2031**, then I'd be 29 with no clear map.
Site years and **judgement** should be the last things to go.
do: Finish the master's and take a **site-based job**, aiming to be chartered by about 2029.
Learn an approved **AI tool** in year one and save most of my pay.
feel: **Uneasy**; there's runway, but 2031 and being 29 weigh on her.
S3.quote: With 2 years I'd be rushing for the nearest safe thing, here I can choose the firm.
fieldNote: Extra time restores her **preference** for a planned route, and she stays in the master's.
Savings are about **independence** from her parents, not fear of poverty.
Age **29** is her specific anxiety marker.

steps.text: Finish the master's and then take a site-based graduate job
Complete the chartership route by about 2029
Learn the firm's approved AI checker in my first year
Save most of my pay toward a small flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generation of work. I'd tell friends to treat it as a long project with milestones, not a catastrophe. And I'd say we should push our unions and councils to plan for it now while it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 34, with ten years of sites, maybe a team under me. The danger is complacency, so I'd have to make sure I'm still learning, even though I hate being told that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, build a decade of site and design experience, and stay in the union all the way. I'd pick up AI tools gradually, one a year, the way I learn design codes. And I'd put money away and maybe study something sideways, like project management, by about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A decade lets me be the person I wanted to be, slowly. I still can't fully shake a worry that someone younger and quicker will undercut me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still be a person who's slow with new tools. Does a decade change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. With ten years I can take the slow route and still end up competent. Fast change is what scares me, slow change I can absorb one tool at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one, compared with the other pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panic, more craft. I'd spend my first year learning to read a site and talk to contractors, because that's the skill that outlasts. And I'd write down what I learn in my notebook, since maybe that's how I'll stay a person who actually understands things.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long project**, not a catastrophe, and we should plan while it's quiet.
I'd keep pushing the **union** and the council to plan early.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 with a decade of **site experience**, so I'd likely be fine.
My danger is **complacency** and someone quicker undercutting me.
do: Build a decade of **site and design** experience and stay in the union throughout.
Pick up one **AI tool** a year and study project management by about 2030.
feel: Fairly **calm**; a decade lets her be the engineer she wanted to be, slowly.
S4.quote: Fast change is what scares me, slow change I can absorb one tool at a time.
fieldNote: Her whole stance is about **pace**: a decade lets her keep her cautious style.
Names **complacency** as her own risk, which is a self-aware admission.
**Craft** first (reading a site, talking to contractors) is her answer to being outpaced.

steps.text: Build ten years of site and design experience at one firm
Pick up one new AI tool each year at a steady pace
Stay in the engineers' union branch throughout

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one worries me most. Everything I've planned, the master's, the chartership, the slow learning, needs time, and 2028 gives me none. What would help is a real plan from government, wage support for graduates, and my firm promising to keep taking juniors. I'd also want one honest conversation with someone senior about what an engineer actually does when machines do the calculations.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as against technology as I sound. I just hate being told to adopt something because everyone else has. If someone showed me a tool and explained how it can be wrong, I'd happily use it. I'd like that to be the normal way people get introduced to it.

headlineQuote: A bridge doesn't care what the press release says.
portrait: Carla is 24, doing a **master's** in structural engineering at Aldmoor, backed by her bus-driver father and cleaner mother's savings.
She prefers the familiar, **never uses AI** tools, and trusts hand calculations and a union at her back.
Her views lean left: she wants rules, wage support and juniors kept on.
She stays calm when little changes, but gets anxious when time runs short, because her careful style needs years.
Her answer to change is to learn one tool at a time and to get onto real sites.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because her careful, slow route needs years she wouldn't have.
whatWouldHelp: A written **government plan** with wage support, and firms promising to keep hiring juniors.
Someone **explaining** how a tool can be wrong before she is told to use it.
